report.answer_text:
Length: The shutdown ran from October 1 to November 12, 2025, which is 43 calendar days.[1] The Congressional Research Service counts 42 full days without appropriations.[1] It was the longest government-wide shutdown in U.S. history.
How it ended:
The dispute: The central dispute was whether to extend enhanced Affordable Care Act premium tax credits set to expire at the end of 2025. The Senate repeatedly fell short of the 60 votes needed to advance a stopgap bill.[1]
The breakthrough: On Nov. 9, a group of eight Democrats agreed to advance a funding measure as part of a broader agreement to end the shutdown.[2] The Senate passed the amended bill on November 10 by 60-40.[3] The House followed on November 12 by 222-209.[3] President Trump signed it the same day.
What the law did: It provided full-year FY2026 funding for three of the twelve appropriations bills. All other agencies were funded at FY2025 levels through January 30, 2026.[4] It also required back pay for furloughed employees and rescinded shutdown-period layoff notices. It barred new layoffs while the stopgap was in effect.[4]
Health care: The shutdown ended without the health care extensions Democrats were fighting for.[5] Senate Democrats did get a promised vote on the issue by mid-December.[6] That proposal failed in the Senate on December 11, 2025.[3]
